113.title: A blessing for each food
113.hook: bread, grain, wine, tree fruit, earth fruit and everything else each have their own blessing
113.howItsDone: Before eating, observant Jews say the blessing that matches the food, bread, other grain foods, wine, tree fruit, earth fruit, or everything else, and the bread blessing covers the rest of a meal with bread.

segments.voice: Yesterday, baruch, the six words that open almost every blessing. Your line was six words before anything. Now, what comes after the six?

A kitchen table: an apple, a strawberry, a slice of bread, a cookie, a glass of wine and a piece of cheese. Ask someone who keeps the blessings to bless them, and they won't say the same thing six times. They'll say six different endings. The apple gets one; the strawberry gets another. The cookie and the bread differ too, though both are made from flour. It sounds like a quiz. It's really a way of looking at what's on your plate. Today: hamotzi, and its cousins.
screen: `SIX FOODS ON A KITCHEN TABLE.` → `SIX DIFFERENT ENDINGS.` → `A WAY OF LOOKING AT YOUR PLATE.`

segments.voice: After the six opening words, each food gets its own ending. Bread: hamotzi lechem min ha'aretz, who brings forth bread from the earth. The words come from a psalm that says, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation, God makes things grow "to bring forth bread out of the earth." Other grain foods, like cake, cookies or pasta: borei minei mezonot, who creates kinds of nourishment. Wine and grape juice: borei pri hagafen, who creates the fruit of the vine. Fruit from a tree: borei pri ha'etz. Fruit and vegetables from the ground: borei pri ha'adamah, the fruit of the earth. Everything else, cheese, eggs, water, candy: shehakol nihyeh bidvaro, by whose word all things came to be. So the apple gets tree, and the strawberry gets earth, because it grows on a low plant. A banana, surprisingly, gets earth too: its plant isn't a tree in the rabbis' sense, since it doesn't keep its trunk year to year. Why bless food at all? The Talmud notices two verses that seem to disagree. One psalm says: "The earth is the LORD'S, and the fulness thereof." Another says: "the earth hath He given to the children of men." Which is it? The Talmud's answer: before the blessing, it's God's. After the blessing, it's been given to you. Enjoying food without a blessing, the Talmud says, is like making personal use of something set aside for the Temple. The blessing is how the food changes hands. And the endings make you look closely: did this grow on a tree, in the ground, from grain?

segments.voice: Picture the next thing you'll eat and trace it back: a tree, like an apple or an orange; the ground, like a potato, a tomato, a strawberry; grain, like bread or pasta; or something else, like cheese or an egg. Name its category, tree, earth, grain, bread, vine or everything else. If you pray, you can say its blessing when you eat it; if not, just pause and name where it came from.
Hamotzi. Who brings forth bread from the earth: the blessing over bread, one of six endings, each food with its own word.
Your line: each food has its word. Tree, earth, vine, grain, bread, or everything else. Day one hundred thirteen, done.

114.title: A hundred blessings a day (Menachot 43b)
114.hook: the Talmud teaches a person should say a hundred blessings each day
114.howItsDone: Jews who pray the three daily services, with the morning blessings and blessings over food, reach about a hundred blessings a day; on Shabbat some add blessings over fruit or spices to complete the count.

segments.voice: Yesterday, hamotzi and its cousins: tree, earth, vine, grain, bread and everything else. Your line was each food has its word.

People count all kinds of things now. Steps. Calories. Hours of sleep. Minutes of screen time, usually with a little shame attached. Ten thousand steps a day has become a kind of modern commandment, even though the number came from a marketing campaign. Long before step counters, the rabbis of the Talmud set a daily goal too. Not steps. Blessings. A hundred of them, every day. Today: me'ah.
screen: `STEPS, CALORIES, SCREEN TIME.` → `TEN THOUSAND STEPS.` → `A HUNDRED BLESSINGS.`

segments.voice: You met this idea in passing on day fifteen. Here's where it lives: a single line in the Talmud, in a discussion about something else entirely. Rabbi Meir says a person is obligated to say a hundred blessings every day. His proof is a piece of wordplay. In Deuteronomy, Moses asks the people, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "And now, Israel, what doth the LORD thy God require of thee." In Hebrew, what is mah. Rabbi Meir reads it as if it were me'ah, a hundred. What does God ask of you? A hundred. Later tradition added a story: in King David's time, a hundred people were dying every day from a plague, David set a hundred blessings a day, and the dying stopped. It's told as tradition; the Bible itself doesn't say it. How do you get to a hundred? It's not as hard as it sounds, if you pray the daily services. The morning blessings alone are over a dozen: for waking, for eyes that see, for clothes, for the ground under your feet. The central standing prayer has nineteen blessings, said three times a day. Add the blessings before and after food, Asher Yatzar after using the bathroom, and the others, and a person who prays the full day reaches about a hundred. On Shabbat the standing prayer is shorter, so some people eat an extra piece of fruit or smell spices to make up the count. Counting thanks the way a watch counts steps. And even if you never say a formal blessing, the idea travels: a hundred times a day, notice something you didn't make, and say so.

segments.voice: Thank you for this breath: that's one. For the chair holding you up, two; for your eyes or your ears, whichever is bringing you this, three. Keep going quietly at your own pace, water, a person, a memory, light, a roof, counting on your fingers if you like, and see how far you get.
Me'ah. A hundred, heard inside the word mah, what, behind Rabbi Meir's daily count of a hundred blessings a day.
Your line: a hundred small thanks. A hundred adds up faster than you'd think. That's day one hundred fourteen.

115.title: Blessing after eating (Deuteronomy 8:10)
115.hook: the one blessing the Torah itself commands: eat, be satisfied, and bless
115.howItsDone: After a meal with bread, observant Jews say Birkat Hamazon, often led by one person when three or more have eaten together; after other foods they say a shorter blessing.

segments.voice: Yesterday, me'ah, the word for a hundred, read two ways. Your line was a hundred small thanks.

The last plate of a big meal. Thanksgiving, a wedding, a birthday dinner. Belts feel tight. Someone's already clearing the table. Everybody's drifting toward the couch or the car. A hungry person will thank anyone for a piece of bread. A full one tends to forget. Here's a surprise about Jewish blessings over food: the blessings before eating were set by the rabbis. The one blessing the Torah itself commands comes after. Today: Birkat Hamazon, the blessing after eating.
screen: `THE LAST PLATE OF A BIG MEAL.` → `A FULL PERSON TENDS TO FORGET.` → `THE TORAH COMMANDS THE AFTER.`

segments.voice: The verse is in Deuteronomy, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "And thou shalt eat and be satisfied, and bless the LORD thy God for the good land which He hath given thee." Eat. Be satisfied. Then bless. A few verses later, the Torah warns: when you've eaten and are satisfied, and built good houses, and your flocks and silver and gold have grown, be careful that your heart doesn't grow proud and forget. The Torah's worry is plain: hunger remembers, fullness forgets. So the blessing sits right at the moment you're most likely to skip it. Birkat hamazon means the blessing for food. It's a longer grace, with four main blessings, and the Talmud gives each one a history. The first, for God who feeds the whole world, it credits to Moses, when the manna fell. The second, for the land, to Joshua, when the people entered it. The third, for Jerusalem, to David and Solomon. The fourth, for God who is good and does good, the rabbis added after a terrible defeat, when the bodies of the fallen were finally allowed burial: a thanks said even out of grief. So one after-dinner grace carries the whole story from the desert to the rabbis. When three or more eat together, one person invites the others to bless, and they answer, like a small congregation around a table. On Shabbat and holidays the custom is to begin by singing a psalm about coming home from exile. After smaller snacks there are shorter blessings. But the idea is the same: when you're full, that's the moment to say thank you.
screen: `EAT, BE SATISFIED, AND BLESS.` · `FULLNESS MAKES YOU FORGET.` · `FOUR BLESSINGS, FOUR HISTORIES.` · `THREE AT A TABLE: LET US BLESS.` · then, large: `FULL, THEN GRATEFUL.`

segments.voice: Think back to the last thing you ate: where did it come from, who grew it, carried it, cooked it, and how did it feel to be full, or at least not hungry? If you pray, you can offer thanks to God for it now, in your own words, or with the old verse: eat, be satisfied, and bless. If you don't, simply thank whoever made the meal possible, in your mind.
Birkat Hamazon. The blessing after eating: the one food blessing the Torah itself commands, said when you're full.
Your line: full, then grateful. The Torah's own food blessing waits until after the meal. See you tomorrow.

116.title: For firsts
116.hook: a blessing for new things, new seasons and first times each year
116.carry: you kept me alive for this
116.howItsDone: Jews say Shehecheyanu on the first night of festivals, at the first Hanukkah candle, over a fruit's first eating in its season, over significant new clothes or a new home, and at many of life's firsts.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Birkat Hamazon, the blessing after eating. Your line was full, then grateful.

The first strawberries of the summer. The first snow. The first time you hold a baby niece. The first night in a new apartment, eating takeout on the floor because the table hasn't arrived. A first can carry a quiet thought under the joy: I made it to this. Not everyone did. Some years it wasn't certain. Jewish tradition has a blessing for exactly that thought, short enough to say in a doorway. Today: Shehecheyanu.
screen: `THE FIRST STRAWBERRIES.` → `THE FIRST NIGHT IN A NEW PLACE.` → `I MADE IT TO THIS.`

segments.voice: After the six opening words, the blessing says: shehecheyanu, v'kiyemanu, v'higianu lazman hazeh. Who has kept us alive, and sustained us, and brought us to this time. Three verbs. Kept us alive: you're still here. Sustained us: held up through everything in between. Brought us to this season: this exact moment. When is it said? The Talmud and later law list many moments. The first night of each festival, over the candles or the wine. The first lighting of the Hanukkah candles. A fruit eaten for the first time in its season: the first cherries, the first pomegranate of the year. Important new clothes, a new home, major new things you're glad of. A close friend you haven't seen in thirty days. And people say it at life's firsts: a baby's birth, a graduation, a wedding, the first time they do something they never thought they'd get to. Notice what the blessing isn't about. Not the strawberry being good, or the dress being nice. It's about time. There was a season when this was out of reach, and I've been carried here. Jewish law even allows saying it on just seeing a new fruit, because the joy is in the arrival, though the usual custom is to wait for the first bite. And on the second night of Rosh Hashanah, there's a custom of setting out a fruit not yet tasted that year, so the blessing has a clear reason to be said.
screen: `KEPT ALIVE, SUSTAINED, BROUGHT HERE.` · `FESTIVALS, FRUIT, NEW CLOTHES.` · `LIFE'S FIRSTS.` · `A BLESSING ABOUT TIME.` · then, large: `BROUGHT US TO THIS SEASON.`

segments.voice: Think back over this season and pick one first: the first cold morning, a first conversation, a first bite of something, a first day without pain, a first attempt at something. Remember when it was out of reach. If you pray, say the blessing, or just its English, who kept us alive and brought us to this time; if you don't, say it plainly: I made it to this.
Shehecheyanu. Who has kept us alive, sustained us, and brought us to this time: the blessing for firsts and new seasons.
Your line: you kept me alive for this. A blessing about time, not things. Day one hundred sixteen, done.

117.title: Blessings for wonders
117.hook: there are blessings for lightning, thunder, the sea, a rainbow and trees in blossom
117.carry: the world has blessings built in
117.howItsDone: Jews say short blessings on seeing lightning, hearing thunder, seeing the sea or a rainbow, and once a year on seeing fruit trees in blossom in the spring month of Nisan.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shehecheyanu, the blessing for firsts. Your line was you kept me alive for this.

You're driving home in a summer storm. The sky goes white for half a second, and the counting starts: one Mississippi, two Mississippi. Then the thunder rolls over the car. Or a beach at the end of a long drive, and there it is, the whole sea at once. Or a rainbow, and everyone in the parking lot pulls out a phone. Nobody plans these moments. Jewish tradition wrote blessings for many of them anyway, ready before they arrive. Today: ma'aseh vereishit.
screen: `THE SKY GOES WHITE.` → `THE WHOLE SEA AT ONCE.` → `EVERYONE PULLS OUT THEIR PHONES.`

segments.voice: The Mishnah, the early collection of rabbinic law, lists them, and the Talmud and later law sort out the endings. Each starts with the six words. In common practice, for lightning and for great mountains: oseh ma'aseh vereishit, who makes the work of creation. As if the world is still being made, right now, in front of you. For thunder, and in the Mishnah's list also earthquakes and fierce winds: shekocho u'gevurato malei olam, whose strength and might fill the world. For the great sea, seen after a long while: who made the great sea. For a rainbow, a blessing that remembers the promise after the flood: who remembers the covenant, is faithful to it, and keeps his word. The story in Genesis says, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "I have set My bow in the cloud." Some even teach not to stare at a rainbow too long, out of respect. And once a year, in the spring month of Nisan, on first seeing fruit trees in blossom, there's a blessing for God, who left nothing lacking in the world, and created good creatures and good trees for people to enjoy. Some go out looking for a blossoming tree just to say it. A psalm names what they share: "How manifold are Thy works, O LORD! In wisdom hast Thou made them all." And a quiet point hides inside the list. Nobody schedules lightning. The words are ready before the storm comes, so the surprise and the answer can arrive together.
screen: `LIGHTNING: THE WORK OF CREATION.` · `THUNDER: STRENGTH FILLS THE WORLD.` · `THE RAINBOW: A PROMISE KEPT.` · `TREES IN BLOSSOM, ONCE A YEAR.` · then, large: `HOW MANIFOLD ARE THY WORKS.`

segments.voice: Look out a window if there is one, or close your eyes and listen: the sky, a cloud, a tree, a bird, the light on a wall, rain. Let something ordinary surprise you, as if you'd never seen it. If you pray, offer one of the old endings, who makes the work of creation; if you don't, simply say wow, and mean it.
Ma'aseh vereishit. The work of creation, the phrase opening the blessing for lightning and great mountains, as if the world is still being made, right now.
Your line: the world has blessings built in. Lightning, seas, rainbows, blossoms, each with its own words. Until tomorrow.

118.title: Blessing on seeing people
118.hook: blessings exist for seeing a great scholar, a ruler, or a friend not seen in a year
118.howItsDone: Jews say special blessings on seeing an outstanding Torah scholar, a great scholar of any people, or a head of state, and on seeing a close friend after thirty days (Shehecheyanu) or after twelve months (mechayeh hametim).

segments.voice: Yesterday, ma'aseh vereishit: lightning, thunder, the sea, the rainbow, trees in blossom. Your line was the world has blessings built in. Today, the wonders walk on two legs.

The arrivals hall at an airport, late afternoon. The doors slide open, and someone comes through pulling a suitcase, looking around. Across the rope, someone else spots them and lights up. They haven't seen each other in a year, maybe longer. A shout, a run, a hug that nearly knocks the suitcase over. It doesn't look like a religious moment. The Talmud has a blessing for it anyway, and its words are startling. Today: mechayeh hametim.
screen: `THE ARRIVALS HALL.` → `A YEAR SINCE THEY LAST MET.` → `THE TALMUD HAS A BLESSING.`

segments.voice: The Talmud lists blessings for seeing people, the way it lists blessings for seeing the sea. For a great Torah scholar, you bless God, who has shared of his wisdom with those who revere him. For a great scholar who isn't Jewish, there's a blessing too: who has given of his wisdom to flesh and blood. So the rabbis built into daily life a blessing for learning wherever it shows up, in anyone. There are matching blessings on seeing a king or a ruler: who has shared of his glory, and who has given of his glory to flesh and blood. You bless not the person, but the source of what you see in them. Now the friend. Seeing a close friend after thirty days, you say Shehecheyanu, the blessing for firsts: who kept us alive and brought us to this time. After more than twelve months, the Talmud says something bigger: blessed is the one who revives the dead. Mechayeh hametim, the same phrase from the daily prayer about God's power to give life back. The rabbis aren't saying the friend was dead. The Talmud gives its own reason for the twelve months: the dead are forgotten from the heart only after a year. So after a year apart, it treats a reunion like being given someone back. A hug in an airport can be a blessing, and so can a Shabbat dinner, or walking into the room where an old friend is waiting.
screen: `A GREAT SCHOLAR: WISDOM SHARED.` · `ANY SCHOLAR: WISDOM GIVEN.` · `A RULER: GLORY GIVEN.` · `A FRIEND AFTER A YEAR.` · then, large: `WHO REVIVES THE DEAD.`

segments.voice: Let a face come to mind, someone you haven't seen or spoken to in a long time; picture them laughing, and remember one thing you love about them. Now picture seeing them again: the doorway, the hug, what you'd say first. If you pray, you can bless the one who gave you this person.
Mechayeh hametim. Who revives the dead: the blessing said on seeing a friend after a year apart, as if given back to you.
Your line: seeing you is a blessing. Wisdom, glory and old friends all have their words. That's day one hundred eighteen.

119.title: Hard news
119.hook: on hearing of a death, Jews bless "the true judge", a blessing inside grief
119.howItsDone: On hearing of a death, many Jews say Baruch Dayan HaEmet; close mourners say the full blessing when they tear their garment (keriah) at the funeral, and visitors to a shiva house traditionally wait for the mourner to speak first.

segments.voice: Yesterday, mechayeh hametim, and a friend after a year. Your line was seeing you is a blessing. That ends a week of blessings: for food, after food, for firsts, for wonders, for people. Today, a harder one.

The phone rings at an odd hour, or a message starts with I'm so sorry. Someone has died. The mind goes blank, or it races. People reach for words and find the wrong ones: everything happens for a reason, at least they're not suffering, I know how you feel. Silence is hard to bear, so people fill it. Jewish tradition has words for this moment too, just three of them, said on hearing of a death. Then, just as important, a way of saying nothing more. Today: Dayan HaEmet.
screen: `A CALL AT AN ODD HOUR.` → `THE WRONG WORDS.` → `THREE WORDS, THEN SILENCE.`

segments.voice: Baruch Dayan HaEmet means blessed is the true judge. The Mishnah says that on good news, you bless the one who is good and does good, and on bad news, you bless the true judge. Then it adds something startling: a person is obligated to bless over the bad just as over the good. That doesn't mean pretending the bad is good. The blessing doesn't say this is fine, and it explains nothing. It says, in the worst moment: God is still God, and I'm still speaking to God, even through this. Many say the short form, those three words, on hearing of a death. Close mourners say the full blessing, with God's name, at the funeral, when they tear a piece of their clothing, keriah, an ancient sign of grief. People often think of Job, who lost everything: "the LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD." Then, the silence. When the priest Aaron lost two sons, the Torah says: "And Aaron held his peace." When Job's friends came to comfort him, they sat with him on the ground for seven days without a word, because they saw how great his pain was. Their trouble started when they began to explain. Mourning customs still carry this. At a shiva house, where mourners sit for seven days, visitors traditionally wait for the mourner to speak first. You arrive with your presence, not a speech. Three words of blessing, then no explanations at all.
screen: `BLESSED IS THE TRUE JUDGE.` · `BLESS OVER THE BAD AS THE GOOD.` · `KERIAH: A TORN GARMENT.` · `AARON HELD HIS PEACE.` · then, large: `THE LORD GAVE, AND THE LORD HATH TAKEN AWAY.`

segments.voice: Go gently here. Let someone you've lost come to mind, or a loss of another kind, or someone else's grief you've witnessed, and don't look for the reason; just let it sit beside you, the way Job's friends sat beside him on the ground. If you pray, you can say the three words, Dayan HaEmet; if you don't, simply let the silence hold it.
Dayan HaEmet. The true judge: the heart of the three words said on hearing of a death, a blessing inside grief that explains nothing.
Your line: even here, a word. Three words, and then presence. I'll see you tomorrow.

original.note: Hebrew: blessed is the true judge. emet, truth, is spelled with the first, middle and last letters of the alphabet.
